title: Console width off by one on some terminals / ssh
body:
On some consoles the output width seems to be calculated one character too wide. See the following example:
```
>>> from rich.console import Console
>>> from rich.table import Table
>>> c = Console()
>>> t = Table("Yo!", "Tables!")
>>> t.add_row("a", "row")
>>> t.add_row("another", "row")
>>> c.print(t)
┏━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┓

┃ Yo!     ┃ Tables! ┃

┡━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━┩

│ a       │ row     │

│ another │ row     │

└─────────┴─────────┘

>>> c = Console(width=c.width-1)
>>> c.print(t)
┏━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Yo!     ┃ Tables! ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━┩
│ a       │ row     │
│ another │ row     │
└─────────┴─────────┘
```
I played around a bit and tested some combinations, some seem fine, others not:

- ssh terminal in vscode: OK
- ssh terminal in ConEmu: one too wide
- ssh terminal in Windows command interpreter (Win+R, cmd): one too wide

Source System is Win10, the system the console runs on was either Ubuntu 18 or Oracle Linux

A possible workaround is as shown above: get a Console, and then get another one which is one narrower than the first one.

Looking ath the code, i understand that you are retrieving the terminal size via `shutil.get_terminal_size()`, so maybe that issue is beyond the reach of the lib.

title: Issue with `end` parameter
body:
I'm looking for a way to write something to my terminal without automatically taking a newline. With the `print` builtin, I can pass an empty string as the `end` paramter. The `end` parameter in `Console.print` doesn't seem to work in the same way however.

**Example:**
```python
print(".", end="")
print(".", end="")
print(".", end="")

console.print(".", end="")
console.print(".", end="")
console.print(".", end="")
```

**Output:**
```
....
.
.
```

**Expected output:**
```
......
```

It also seems to add a space before the `end` character:

**Example:**
```python
print(".", end="x")
console.print(".", end="x")
```

**Output:**
```
.x. x
```

**Expected output:**
```
.x.x
```

title: `sep` parameter is inconsistent with builtin `print`
body:
`sep` behaves differently from builtin print. I don't know if this is intentional or not, but the behaviour is slightly different from how the docs describe it. (I didn't expect the `sep` to be added to the *end* of the string, only *between* the printed items).

**Example:**
```python
print(".", ".", sep="a")
console.print(".", ".", sep="a")
```

**Output:**
```
.a.
.a.a
```

**Expected output:**
```
.a.
.a.
```

title: Automatic Jupyter environment detection
body:
Something similar to tqdm's [`auto`](https://github.com/tqdm/tqdm/blob/master/tqdm/auto.py) module would be helpful. This would mean I can run the same code in Jupyter or a terminal and get the same `rich` experience.

Basically, it would just be a small wrapper that does a simple check to whether or not we are in an IPython environment or a regular Python one, and then import the `console` and `print` objects from the correct package. Then you could write code like this, knowing it would work wherever it was run:

```python
from rich.auto import print

print("[bold magenta]Hello, world![\]")
```

Alternatively you could put this functionality into the default imports; I'm not sure why you would ever not want this (other than to avoid the overhead of checking, but that's fairly minimal).

title: Integrate into existing logging seamlessly
body:
```Python3
def setup_logger(level, filename, mode, encoding='utf8',
                 fmt=None, size=0, count=0):

title: Deadlock when exiting Progress context
body:
I can consistently reproduce this by letting the following script run. Eventually the progress bars will hang when they're nearly full, like so:

![deadlock](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/43117506/82743832-85102500-9d25-11ea-8a92-8b8472f12dde.png)

```python
from rich.progress import track
from rich.progress import Progress
import random
import time

while True:
    with Progress() as progress:
        task1 = progress.add_task(f"[red]Downloading...", total=10)
        task2 = progress.add_task("[green]Processing...", total=10)
        task3 = progress.add_task("[cyan]Cooking...", total=10)

        while not progress.finished:
            progress.update(task1, advance=random.random())
            progress.update(task2, advance=random.random())
            progress.update(task3, advance=random.random())
            time.sleep(0.1)
```

I believe the problematic sequence of events is as follows:
1. The main thread exits from a `Progress` context and acquires `Progress._lock` in `Progress.__exit__()`
https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/blob/55988c6e721cc03ab4f6dc6aeca3089e7c5c13ae/rich/progress.py#L447-L451

2. The refresh thread finishes waiting on `_RefreshThread.done` and calls `Progress.refresh()`, at which point it starts waiting for `Progress._lock`
https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/blob/55988c6e721cc03ab4f6dc6aeca3089e7c5c13ae/rich/progress.py#L346-L348
https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/blob/55988c6e721cc03ab4f6dc6aeca3089e7c5c13ae/rich/progress.py#L574-L582

3. The main thread calls `Progress._refresh_thread.stop()` in `Progress.stop()`, at which point it waits for the refresh thread to finish with `_RefreshThread.join()`
https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/blob/55988c6e721cc03ab4f6dc6aeca3089e7c5c13ae/rich/progress.py#L422-L436
https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/blob/55988c6e721cc03ab4f6dc6aeca3089e7c5c13ae/rich/progress.py#L342-L344

At this point the main thread is holding `Progress._lock` and waiting on

title: Feature request: Screen re-/storing
body:
I've been playing around with `rich` as of late and I am really enjoying it. :+1:
But there is one thing I wish was also in this wonderful chuck of code and that would be the ability to programmatically store and restore the terminal view (Like how `less` and other common commandline utilities do). I've got a somewhat working version of a decorator that I am using in my current project which I think some other people might find fairly useful. ;)

```python
from contextlib import contextmanager
import subprocess

@contextmanager
def second_screen():
    try:
        r_code, s_code = (
            subprocess.getoutput(
                r"infocmp -1 | grep 'rmcup\|smcup' | sed 's/.*=\(.*\),/\1/'"
            )
            .replace("\\E", "\033")
            .split("\n")
        )
        try:
            print(s_code + "\033[0;0H", end="")
            yield
        finally:
            print(r_code, end="")
            return
    except:
        yield
```

I tried my hand at making it work with multiple different terminals by using `infocmp` to findout the proper escape sequence.

I am unsure if this is something that is considered inside the scope of this library, but imho I think it would by a great addition. I think the best way to integrate this into the API would be to add it as a member of the `Console`-class to enable the following usage:

```python
from rich.console import Console

console = Console()

with console.second_screen():
    console.print("It works!", style="bold green")
```

EDIT: For me the escape sequences turn out to be:
```python
s_code = '\033[?1049h\033[22;0;0t'
r_code = '\033[?1049l\033[23;0;0t'
```
So switch to secondary/primary buffer and re-/store icon and window title from/to stack respectively.

title: Bug: 24-bit color should work on conhost as of Windows 10.0.15063
body:
According to [this blog post](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/commandline/24-bit-color-in-the-windows-console/), the windows console host added support for 24-bit color in build 14931.

It is safer and easier to gate the use of 24-bit color on the Windows version and _not_ the presence of Windows Terminal, especially as WT is not the only terminal emulator that benefits from conhost enhancements.

title: Request: do not use WT_SESSION to detect Windows Terminal
body:
There's a small handful of issues with detecting `WT_SESSION` and using that as an indicator that you can use advanced VT:

* `WT_SESSION` is not an API, and it was my greatest fear when we introduced it that people would use it for feature detection
   * This is why I (so far) refuse to add support for `TERM_PROGRAM` or `TERM_PROGRAM_VERSION`, and would rather us standardize on `TERM` :smile:
* It _will not_ be set by other terminal emulators using the pseudoconsole API (like Visual Studio's terminal, which is built on the WT renderer and where they're considering shipping a copy of OpenConsole down to Windows 10 RS4)
* Everything WT supports is supported by the conhost instance that it uses to back every tab
* Every change to conhost (and therefore WT's VT support) flows back out through the Windows insider program and eventually lands for all console users in the stable builds

It's safer to use feature detection for the console. If you can enable `ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING`, VT is supported; version detection is required for _some things_, unfortunately: if you're beyond 10.0.15063 24-bit color is supported.

title: Suggestion: use stack_data for better tracebacks
body:
Hi! I've recently created a few libraries that are helpful for extracting information from frames and tracebacks, and I think they could be very useful to rich.

- [`executing`](https://github.com/alexmojaki/executing) can identify the exact AST node being executed by a frame in many cases. It's always disappointed me that Python only points to a line in each frame in tracebacks, especially when the expression/statement at fault spans many lines. Sometimes it can be really hard to interpret. Currently [executing is used in IPython](https://github.com/ipython/ipython/pull/12150) (in master, unreleased) to highlight the node, here's what it looks like:

![ipython](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3627481/75476425-3e6b9280-59a3-11ea-9b6c-b9e099475a45.png)

- `executing` can also infer a function `__qualname__` from a code object, meaning your traceback can say `lorem/ipsum.py in MyClass.__init__ at line 123` instead of just `__init__`, which is much more informative.
- [`pure_eval`](https://github.com/alexmojaki/pure_eval) can safely evaluate certain AST nodes without side effects, so that if the source for a frame contains expressions like `self.foo` and `bar[key]` their values can often be shown alongside plain variables. 
- [`stack_data`](https://github.com/alexmojaki/stack_data) collects data from tracebacks for the purpose of formatting and displaying them. It uses `executing` and `pure_eval` and also provides a lot of functionality of its own. [I integrated`stack_data` into IPython](https://github.com/ipython/ipython/pull/11886) which allowed removing a lot of flaky custom introspection code, fixing several bugs and making the code more maintainable.

For rich, I'm thinking you could use stack_data to:

- Reduce the amount of code in the repo.
- More intelligently select which lines of code to display, instead of just a fixed number lines before and after.
- Display the values of local variables and other expressions for each frame in a nic

title: Console.print with f-strings featuring variables containing a list do not print the list
body:
**Describe the bug**
When using Console.print with an f-string featuring variables containing a list, the list does not get printed (but other non-list content from the variable is correctly printed).  It does not occur with a regular print.

**To Reproduce**

````python
from rich.console import Console
console = Console()
results = {'result1':'something', 'result2':[1,2,3]}
print(f'Comment {results}') # this works as expected
# outputs: Comment {'result1': 'something', 'result2': [1, 2, 3]}
console.print(f'Comment {results}') # this nicely colours the structure but it has lost the list
# outputs: Comment {'result1': 'something', 'result2': }
````

**Platform**
Arch Linux on x86_64
Terminal software: Konsole version 20.04.3
Python version: 3.7.6
Rich version: 3.3.2

This is hardly the most critical of issues, and there's an easy work around (`console.print(f'Comment ', results, end='')`) but as it is easy to miss, it might catch some people out if they're not aware of it.

|    10:45 |     17:00 |     6:15 |

|      Clock-in        | Clock-out | Duration |

|                10:45 |     17:00 |     6:15 |

title: [Improvement] progress.track is relatively slow
body:
**Description**
I really like the look and feel of rich.  One thing that stops me using it more is that ```rich.progress.track``` is slow compared to ```tqdm.tqdm```

**To Reproduce**
```python
from rich.progress import track
from time import time
from functools import wraps

import timeit

from tqdm import tqdm

def measure(func):
    """Simple decorator to measure execution time"""
    @wraps(func)
    def _time_it(*args, **kwargs):
        start = int(round(time() * 1000))
        try:
            return func(*args, **kwargs)
        finally:
            end_ = int(round(time() * 1000)) - start
            print(f"Total execution time: {end_ if end_ > 0 else 0} ms")
    return _time_it


@measure
def go_track(count):
    for i in track(range(0, count)):
        pass


@measure
def go_tqdm(count):
    for i in tqdm(range(0, count)):
        pass


count = 1 * 1000 * 1000

print(f"Counting to {count} with rich.progress.track")
go_track(count)
print()
print(f"Counting to {count} with tqdm.tqdm")
go_tqdm(count)
```

title: [REQUEST] Allow ordering of columns for custom logging
body:
At the moment, I would love to convert from colorama to using Rich for my projects. However, I notice that when you define the logging handler, the format of the message is decided by the private class LogRender. Whilst you can turn things on or off in this class, I notice you cannot reorder.

On a similar note, I cannot find any examples of updating the ReprHighlighter and associated new styles in the documentation (though I might have missed it!), and given that they seem to be in different places after digging through the code (the Console object has the styling under the theme, and the syntax matching is done via extending the Highlighter) I feel like this would also be a useful addition! title: [REQUEST] rich.print != rich.console.print
body:
Putting `from rich import print` at the top of your imports is a nice quick way to load in the power of rich without setting up a console and all that.

However, this version of `print` does not expose all of the arguments one gets from `console.print`. `rich.print` provides `sep`, `end`, `file`, and `flush`--presumably because this is intended as a drop-in replacement for Python's own `print` function.

But, I don't think there is a technical reason why it cannot also include `highlight`, `overflow`, and all the rest. Perhaps it's because one might do this and then hope it will still work everywhere:

```python
try:
    from rich import print
except ImportError:
    pass

print("This still works")
print("But this doesn't", justify='right')
```

**How would you improve Rich?**

Oh sure, one could do this:

```python
from rich.console import Console
console = Console()
print = console.print
print('But this is clunky', justify='right')
```

But, maybe offering the extended version of `print` without having to set up a console is better? Perhaps:

```python
from rich import superprint as print
print("This still works")
print("So does this!", justify='right')
```

title: [BUG] use of stderr colorize trick breaks ability to produce ANSI on stderr
body:
**Describe the bug**
While this is an unlikely advanced use-case, I should better mention it, in hope we can find a workaround for it.

There is a shell trick that is used by some users in order to colorize output received on stderr with a different color, making easier to distinguish nature of output for programs producing output on both streams.

There are several implementations available as it may differ a little bit between platforms or shells but it mainly looks like https://github.com/cehoffman/dotfiles/blob/master/zsh/config#L174-L193  

What happens is that stderr is redirected to an unnamed pipe before being added an ANSI coloring sequence for each line. 

This works fine with one exception: programs that verify `sys.stderr.isatty()` as a side effect of this approach is that this is no longer reports true.

Programs that do use only `sys.stdout.isatty()` to determine if ANSI is supported or not are not affected, as ANSI still works on stderr.

I am not yet sure which is the best approach to avoid this issue as I see pros and cons for all cases. I do see some users wanting to avoid ANSI on stderr, for example if they redirect output for log files.

title: [Suggestion] Use binary prefixes instead of decimal ones
body:
I was tinkering with progress bars and noticed the file size unit is expressed with [decimal prefixes](https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/blob/33a171d72013f470c0edb5f61e226ca80729cbf6/rich/progress.py#L301) (i.e. KB, MB, GB, etc.) while the actual number is expressed as binary. I suggest you to consider switching to binary prefixes (i.e. KiB, MiB, GiB, etc.) in order to have consistency with the number and its unit of measure and to remove the ambiguity regarding in which base the prefix is expressed: KiB, MiB, etc. are used exclusively with powers of 2, while I've seen KB, MB, etc. used with powers of 10 (as they should be) and powers of 2 (as in this case, but generally in casual conversations).
For instance, I tried with a file with a size of 6'988'379 bytes. Expressed in MiB it's 6,7 and this is the number printed by the progress bar, while in MB it's 6,9. As you can notice, while dealing with MiB vs MB the difference is ~5%, but when the size is bigger it can be ~7% (GiB vs GB), ~10% (TiB vs TB) and so on, so please consider using only one format.

title: [REQUEST] Respect PY_COLORS environment variable
body:
`PY_COLORS` is a [very popular](https://github.com/search?l=&q=PY_COLORS&type=code) method for forcing ANSI mode on or off in a command line application. 

Basically undefined means keeping application default behavior, likely auto-detection. Having it `PY_COLORS=0` means application will not use any ANSI codes and `PY_COLORS=1` will force ANSI mode regardless if terminal reports it or not.

For me personally is not a big deal as I already have code in applications I work with, but it would prove useful to have this directly into rich, so any user of rich would get this for free.

An implementation example can be seen at https://github.com/ansible-community/molecule/blob/20e1fa8a23308a9103e2dbdb4d3c4ae1ffe59c9d/molecule/logger.py#L42-L48

That is very useful feature to have when running on CI as you do not want to end-up defining 50-100 environment variables only to control ANSI behavior.

title: [REQUEST] Default padding for panels
body:
**How would you improve Rich?**

At the moment panels have no default padding:

```python
>>> from rich import print
>>> from rich.panel import Panel
>>> print(Panel.fit("Hello World!"))
╭────────────╮
│Hello World!│
╰────────────╯
```

I propose adding a default left and right padding to make the output more aesthetically pleasing:

```python
>>> print(Panel.fit("Hello World!", padding=(0, 1)))
╭──────────────╮
│ Hello World! │
╰──────────────╯
```

A quirk of most monospace fonts and how characters are often printed in the terminal, means that a padding of `(0, 1)` gives a more even padding than `(0, 0)`.

**What problem does it solved for you?**

This can be solved by the user by simply suppling the `padding` parameter as I have above.

I am aware that this may just be a suggestion to change the default to my personal preference, but I feel that this extra padding means the edge of the text is more evenly centred in the panel than the current default. This would make the default behaviour of `rich` closer to the default behaviour of many other tools, for example:

HTML `<input>` box (on Chrome):

title: [BUG] Failing mypy --strict due to implicit reexports
body:
**Describe the bug**

Mypy raises a no attribute error when run with the `--strict` flag.

**To Reproduce**

Given `file.py`

```python
from rich.console import Measurement

Measurement(10, 100)
```

```sh
%mypy --strict file.py
scratch/unpack.py:1: error: Module 'rich.console' has no attribute 'Measurement'
```

**Platform**

Python: 3.89
macOS: 10.15.6
Rich: 9.0.1

**Discussion**

I saw this issue popping up in a few places.

- [Mypy issue](https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/7030)
- [Typer](https://github.com/tiangolo/typer/issues/112)
- [Typer diff](https://github.com/tiangolo/typer/pull/147/files)

This seems to come up due to the new [`--no-implicit-reexport`](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/command_line.html#cmdoption-mypy-no-implicit-reexport) flag.

The solution seems to be to go from this

```python
from foo import bar
```

to either of these

```python
from foo import bar as bar
```

```python
from foo import bar
__all__ = ['bar']
```

in your `__init__.py`

title: Live Display Implementation
body:
There has been [interest](https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/issues?q=is%3Aissue+live) in live updating when it comes to using rich.

## Proposal
The main goal of this is to provide an abstraction of the Progress feature that can be used with any `RenderableType` -- Live. 

## Progress

I'm currently working on this in #382. 

![rich_live_example](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/33010515/95882390-a5c62f00-0d47-11eb-96ea-41ed61971045.gif)

Significant portions of the code and logic from `rich.progress` have been re-used for the implementation.  There is a working example going with some extremely raw tests included `python -m rich.live`

### Potential Areas of Concern
- Lots of duplicate code exists between `Progress` and `Live`
   - Perhaps they should share a common abstract parent class?

title: [BUG] Rich is too restrictive on dataclasses dependency
body:
**Describe the bug**
Few minutes ago I got some [pip install failures](https://github.com/ansible-community/molecule-podman/pull/25/checks?check_run_id=1459010189) which, IMHO are caused by being too restrictive regarding supported versions. 

```
py36:
rich 9.2.0 has requirement dataclasses<0.8,>=0.7; python_version >= "3.6" and python_version < "3.7", but you have dataclasses 0.8.
```

I know a bump happened on on Nov 10 but no release was made since. Still, I do think that the version compatibility range should not have a ceiling bound unless it is already known to break the library.

This is particularly problematic with rich which is mostly a library, so it needs to play well with other dependencies the project may need.

Lets assume you make 9.2.1 hotfix today to sort this issue. What happens if dataclasses makes release 0.9 tomorrow, it will likely get into conflict with rich again, even if there is no proof that they do not work together. This is even more problematic as the ceiling seams to be applied to the minor version.

If the concerns around possible breakage produced by dataclasses are real, at least the conditions should look more like `<1.0`.

title: [REQUEST] Add a `disable` argument for progress bar
body:
**How would you improve Rich?**

In tqdm there is a `disable` argument to disable the progress bar.

```
disable: bool, optional
Whether to disable the entire progress bar wrapper [default: False]. If set to None, disable on non-TTY.
```

This is very useful for some applications to control output verbosity. Otherwise, an if statement is needed which makes the code dirty.

Before using `disable`

```python
from rich.progress import track

if verbosity:
    for i in range(100):
        print(i)
else:
    for i in track(range(100)):
        print(i)
```

If we have `disable`

```python
from rich.progress import track

for i in track(range(100), disable=verbosity):
    print(i)
```

title: [REQUEST] Change dependencies constraints from ^ to >=
body:
Have you checked the issues for a similar suggestions?

Yes, did not find a similar request.

**How would you improve Rich?**

Make rich less likely to cause dependency resolution issues. For example, currently you have a caret dependency on colorama ^0.4.0. Your package is young enough so that this covers all newer versions. But if colorama outputs a version 0.5.0, and another package would use ^0.5.0, this would lead to an unresolvable dependency - and that although very likely there is no issue at all. 

The caret operator is very conservative, assumes a strict adherence to SemVer on the side of the dependency that is often not the case.

**What problem does it solved for you?**

Forward looking action to prevent dependency resolution problems in the future for projects with many dependencies. Other languages can use ^ much better as they allow multiple versions of the same package to be installed, but python doesn't. So ^ will over the long run lead to incompatible dependencies.

body:

Since I cannot directly modify the training loop I need to use a class `CustomLogger` method which is called at each iteration. 
This class stores the total length `train_data_len` of the loop and the called method  `on_batch_end`.
I would like to define a progress class attribute and update it everytime the method is called, like the following:

```

class CustomLogger(Callback):
    def __init__(
        self, train_data_len=None, eval_data_len=None, logging_step=50
    ):

        self.train_data_len = train_data_len
        self.eval_data_len = eval_data_len
        # define the progress class and add train and eval
        self.progress = Progress()
        self.train_p = self.progress.add_task("Train", total=self.train_data_len)
        self.eval_p = self.progress.add_task("Eval", total=self.eval_data_len)

title: [BUG] Output is hard-wrapped when passed through a pipe
body:
**Describe the bug**
This might be a duplicate of #119 but I'm opening it just in case because of the new `soft_wrap` option.

We are piping output from a program using Rich (specifically a Rich table) to another program. [Rich was correctly soft-wrapping when not being piped, but hard-wrapping at 80 chars when piped.](https://github.com/standardebooks/tools/issues/382) This makes it hard to process output through a pipe, because usually in a pipe we don't want any wrapping at all and we don't know in advance how wide the output might be. (In our case we always want the output to be as wide as the user's terminal, because the output is very verbose.)

I tried passing `force_terminal`, both `True` and `False`, to `Console()` and the newer `soft_wrap=True` option to `console.print()` but neither did what I was expecting, and piped output was still hard-wrapped.

Using `COLUMNS` isn't a great solution because we don't want any wrapping and we don't know how long the output might be.

Is `soft_wrap` supposed to solve this, and maybe there is a bug when using it to print tables? Or is this just not possible at all?

If `soft_wrap` is meant to solve this, then we can simply detect if we're in a pipe and pass that option accordingly. But if not, it would be very helpful to be able to specify `really_no_hard_wrapping_at_all_please` for cases like this. Piping output is a common use case and it is surprising to have output soft-wrapped at the CLI but hard-wrapped in a pipe.

**To Reproduce**
```python
console = Console()

table = Table(show_header=True, header_style="bold", show_lines=True)
table.add_column("Code", width=5, no_wrap=True)
table.add_column("Severity", no_wrap=True)

title: [BUG] Console.out() always enables highlighting by default
body:
`Console.out()` by default enables highlighting even if it is disabled in the Console constructor.

```python
from rich.console import Console
console = Console(highlight=False)
console.print('cd /usr/lib')  # no hightlight
console.out('cd /usr/lib')  # hightlight
```

It is expected that `Console.out()` makes less changes to the output than `Console.print()`.

It happens because the default value of *hightlight* is `True` in `Console.out()` and `None` in `Console.print()`. The fix is making it `None`.

rich 9.3.0

title: [BUG] Conflict between rich progress and click.echo()
body:
There is a conflict between `rich.progress.Progress` and `click.echo()`.

The `rich.progress.Progress` context manager monkey-patches `sys.stdout`. `click.echo()` detects whether `sys.stdout` is a text stream or byte stream (this is questionable, but it is a different issue) by trying to write an empty bytes object. If the test is passed successfully, then it is a bytes stream, and click encodes string before writing it. But the wrapper instantiated by Progress ignores empty input for `write()`, including empty bytes object, therefore `click.echo()` concludes that it is a byte stream.

Example:
```python
import click
from rich.progress import Progress
with Progress():
    click.echo('test')
```
Traceback:
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File ".../site-packages/click/utils.py", line 272, in echo
    file.write(message)
  File ".../site-packages/rich/progress.py", line 491, in write
    line, new_line, text = text.partition("\n")
TypeError: a bytes-like object is required, not 'str'
```

It is not completely a failure of rich, but it would be better if the wrapper better emulate output text stream. In particularly check that the argument of `write()` is string.

rich 9.3.0

title: [REQUEST]  Add TimeElapsedColumn class for Progress
body:
Have you checked the issues for a similar suggestions? Yes

**How would you improve Rich?**

Please add a Time Elapsed as a standard column for the Progress bar feature.
```
class TimeElapsedColumn(ProgressColumn):
    """Renders elapsed time."""

    # Only refresh twice a second to prevent jitter
    max_refresh = 0.5

    def render(self, task: "Task") -> Text:
        """Show time elapsed."""
        elapsed = task.elapsed
        if elapsed is None:
            return Text("-:--:--", style="progress.remaining")
        elapsed_delta = timedelta(seconds=int(elapsed))
        return Text(str(elapsed_delta), style="progress.remaining")
```
This snippet is refactored from the TimeRemainingColumn class.  An update to the default style may need to also be considered.

**What problem does it solved for you?**
Seeing time Elapsed on long progress jobs is useful for understanding where the long running parts of the application are, and for the user to accept accuracy of the Time Remaining value.

Also, this would close the gap of similar metadata available on the default display of tqdm.  That could reduce an import.

title: [BUG] print sometimes ignores \r escape sequence
body:
**Describe the bug**
Rich doesn't appear to take notice of the `\r` escape sequence when it's included with a string as an argument to `rich.print`. If it's used in the `end` argument, it works as expected.

**To Reproduce**
```py
from rich import print as rprint

# behaviour with rich
rprint("Hello world!", end="\r")
rprint("Hi there, world!")

rprint("Hello world!\r", end="")
rprint("Hi there, world!")

print()

# standard behaviour
print("Hello world!", end="\r")
print("Hi there, world!")

print("Hello world!\r", end="")
print("Hi there, world!")
```

Outputs:

```cmd

title: [BUG] Markup escaping not working as expected
body:
**Describe the bug**
It's a bit of an edge case, but right now it's not possible to output a backslash immediately before a square bracket starting a markup token. While it does properly output a single backslash if you feed in `r'\\'` followed by a markup token, it still disables interpreting the token as markup.

**To Reproduce**
Working cases:

`rich.print(r'[bold]text[/]')`  prints "**text**"
`rich.print(r'\[not a tag]')`  prints "[not a tag]"

Not working case:
`rich.print(r'\\[bold]some text[/]')`  gives an error about an unexpected close tag, because it doesn't treat "[bold]" as markup. The expected result here was "\\**text**", a single backslash followed by the text in bold.

Adding more backslashes also produces a surprising result. It seems like the rightmost backslash is always consumed to disable markup on the square bracket, but all the previous backslashes are passed through as-is, rather than having every other backslash escape the following one. So, with three backslashes, I was expecting one to be output (consuming the first two of the input) and one to be left over to escape the square bracket and disable markup. WIth four backslashes, I was expecting two backslashes to be output (consuming all four of the input) and the square bracket after that to be treated as markup.

**Platform**
Rich 9.5.1 on macOS Mojave (10.14.6) with Apple's Terminal.app.

title: [BUG] Setting color_system seems to affect more than just color
body:
**Describe the bug**
I was experimenting with setting force_terminal and color_system on a Console object and got some unexpected results. I was expecting that setting force_terminal to False would suppress all rich text styling and color and that setting force_terminal to True and color_system to False would only disable color, but not disable things like bold or italics.

Instead, what I got was that setting color_system to None seems to disable all color _and_ styling, and setting color_system to anything but None (such as 'standard' or '256') seems to enable both color and styling, regardless of what force_terminal is set to.

**To Reproduce**
I was expecting the following output:

```python
from rich.console import Console
c = Console(force_terminal=True, color_system=None)
c.print('[red bold]Expecting bold but not red[/]')

c = Console(force_terminal=False, color_system='standard')
c.print('[red bold]Expecting neither red nor bold[/]')
```

What I actually get is neither red nor bold for the first case (disabling more than just color), and both red and bold for the second case (outputting both color and styling even though there's no terminal):

![Screen Shot 2021-01-05 at 8 29 38 PM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1901085/103729212-bed02c00-4f94-11eb-9451-58f30819d28f.png)

The first set of output here is neither red nor bold, and the second set is both red & bold.

Setting force_terminal to both False and True works ok with color_system as 'auto'. However, once color_system is set explicitly, it seems like it overrides the setting of force_terminal, either enabling or disabling both color & styling, rather than only affecting color.

**Platform**
Rich 9.5.1 on macOS Mojave (10.14.6) with Apple's Terminal.app.

title: [BUG] from rich import traceback points to builtin
body:
Ohai. My first bug report, I think.

**Describe the bug**
The docs state that the way to install traceback or pretty is in this form:

```
from rich.traceback import install
install()
```
In pretty much all my scripts, in order to install both traceback and pretty, I prefer to do something like this in order to keep the namespaces from colliding. 

```
from rich import pretty, traceback
traceback.install(show_locals=True)
pretty.install()
```

This usually works because import orders know that traceback and pretty are coming from the rich module. However, with the new changes made in recent PRs in how the imports for traceback are working, Python resolves `from rich import traceback` as the built-in traceback module instead, therefore the code above fails with an `AttributeError: module 'traceback' has no attribute install` since it's the wrong module completely. It's likely because with the new changes `traceback` is stomping `rich.traceback`.

**To Reproduce**

```
from rich import traceback
traceback.install()
```

**Platform**
What platform (Win/Linux/Mac) are you running on? What terminal software are you using?

Windows 10/Windows Terminal/Rich 9.10.0

**Thoughts**
Although the way I'm doing it isn't how the docs describe (👀), the import order should generally be preserved to return the expected module. `from rich import traceback` should be expected to return `rich.traceback`.

title: [REQUEST] Fixed Width Progress Text Column
body:
**How would you improve Rich?**

Give as much detail as you can. Example code of how you would like it to work would help.

I would like a text column in a progress bar to be fixed width. I have created a ProgressColumn object (modified TextColumn) that does just that. I am not sure if there is already a better method of doing so by using the `text.truncate` while construction the `Progress()` class, so I created this.

```python
class SizedTextColumn(ProgressColumn):
    """A column containing text."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        text_format: str,
        style: StyleType = "none",
        justify: JustifyMethod = "left",
        markup: bool = True,
        highlighter: Highlighter = None,
        overflow: Optional[OverflowMethod] = None,
        width: int = 0,
    ) -> None:
        self.text_format = text_format
        self.justify = justify
        self.style = style
        self.markup = markup
        self.highlighter = highlighter
        self.overflow = overflow
        self.width = width
        super().__init__()

    def render(self, task: "Task") -> Text:
        _text = self.text_format.format(task=task)
        if self.markup:
            text = Text.from_markup(_text, style=self.style, justify=self.justify)
        else:
            text = Text(_text, style=self.style, justify=self.justify)
        if self.highlighter:
            self.highlighter.highlight(text)
        if self.width:
            text.truncate(max_width=self.width, overflow=self.overflow, pad=True)
        return text
```

More [here](https://github.com/phcreery/rich)

**What problem does it solved for you?**

It makes the visibility of multiple bars with leading text much easier to comprehend. It is also being used in [PR #1098](https://github.com/spotDL/spotify-downloader/pull/1098) of [spotDL/spotify-downloader](https://github.com/spotDL/spotify-downloader)

title: [REQUEST] Callback before refresh is executed
body:
I have to update a live view quite often.
My input data is up to 100Hz but I want to create the rich tables only when a refresh is executed (e.g. refresh_per_second=10).
Calling update() every-time new data is received doesn't make sense, as only every tenth data will finally be printed to screen.

It would be good to have a callback which is called before refresh() is executed to finally create the tables to display.
In my implementation I did it now by overriding refresh(), but I don't know if anybody else could need this.

````python
class MyRichLive(Live):
    def __init__(
        self,
        refresh_callback,
        **kwargs
    ):
        self.refresh_callback = refresh_callback
        super(MyRichLive, self).__init__(**kwargs)

    def refresh(self) -> None:
        self.refresh_callback()
        super(MyRichLive, self).refresh()
````

title: [REQUEST] Progress bars with undetermined 'total'
body:
Hi. The documentation describes the usage of [indeterminate progress bars](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/progress.html#indeterminate-progress) that displays a waiting animation during the time the number of steps is computed.

![indeterminate state](https://media.moyaproject.com/willmcgugan/uploads/thumbnails/techblog/788d9cb6-9e8f-11ea-b769-f23c91845b44.png/788d9cb6-9e8f-11ea-b769-f23c91845b44png.lg.3.jpeg)

However, sometimes you never know how many steps you except (when reading a stream for instance), but this is something rich does not accept:
https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/blob/1c1d72ccad965a41500253680c73e6606924cd13/rich/progress.py#L667-L673

I suggest in those cases to display a waiting animation instead.

Of course in this case the percentage and the ETA would not be very usable, but the bar could display the number of items processed (this is what tqdm does).

What do you think?

Hi,

I am not sure if it is a bug or intended behavior. But I configured a RichHandler with rich traceback toggled on. I also added a custom formatter to include the process name and Id in all log messages.

Lars

title: [REQUEST] Re-splittable Layouts
body:
I'm playing with some TUI-like ideas using Rich, in particular, adjustable layouts like `tmux` can do. I find myself wanting to change the splits for a layout dynamically.

If I understand the API correctly, once a `Layout` is split using `Layout.split`, there is no way to "unsplit" it - you can call `split` again to add more sub-layouts or change the direction, but you can't "start over". For my own experimentation I've been manually setting `layout._children = []` and then calling `split` again with the new set of children I'd like it to have, like this:

```python
header = Layout(Header(options), name="header", size=1)
footer = Layout(Footer(state=state, options=options), name="footer", size=1)
body = Layout(name="body", ratio=1)

root = Layout(name="root")
root.split(header, body, footer)

def resplit():
    body._children = []
    verts = []
    for group in state.tile_groups:
        v = Layout()
        v.split(*(tile.layout for tile in group), direction="vertical")
        verts.append(v)
    body.split(*verts, direction="horizontal")
```

... which is obviously not part of the public API :)

You can already dynamically change the renderable attached to a `Layout` using `Layout.update`, so I'm imagining a feature that provides a parallel capability for sub-layouts. It seems like the alternative is rebuilding `Layout` from scratch on every refresh, which would certainly work, but since the parents are also split `Layouts`, I would need to build the entire tree. So, this seems like a natural extension of the existing API and would lessen the need to store the desired layout structure externally to Rich.

title: [REQUEST] Add color to custom log levels.
body:
**Have you checked the issues for a similar suggestions?**

I have reviewed #407 (closed) and #419, which allows subclassing the RichHandler, but there is not an obvious way to style levels.

**How would you improve Rich?**

Allow markup of custom log levels provided from the logging module in stdlib.

```python
# Current behavior 
import logging
from rich.logging import RichHandler

logging.basicConfig(
    level=LOG_LEVEL,
    format="%(message)s",
    datefmt="%X",
    handlers=[RichHandler(rich_tracebacks=True, tracebacks_show_locals=True, console=_CONSOLE)],
)
logging.addLevelName(70, "[green]CUSTOM[/]")
logging.log(70, "<MESSAGE>")

"""
Literally prints:
<TIME> [green]CUSTOM[/] <MESSAGE>
"""

# Desired behavior
logging.addLevelName(70, "[green]CUSTOM[/]")

"""
Literally prints (with color):
<TIME> CUSTOM <MESSAGE>
"""
```

**What problem does it solved for you?**

This would allow for more clear custom logging for our plugin-based architecture.

title: [REQUEST] Enable support for OSC8 terminal escape codes
body: > Consider posting in https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/discussions for feedback before raising a feature request. I think it's worth filing a feature request for. > Have you checked the issues for a similar suggestions? Yes **How would you improve Rich?** Rich is GREAT for formatting and coloring text in a terminal, but it does not have support for OSC8 hyperlinks, as supported by e.g. iTerm2. In short OSC8 is a special escape sequence that allows console output to be clickable hyperlinks. In Python, a OSC8 hyperlink can be generated pretty trivially: ```py >>> url='https://google.com' >>> name='Google' >>> print(f'\x1b]8;;{url}\x07{name}\x1b]8;;\x07') Google ``` If you are using a compliant shell (most are, notably Terminal.app on macOS does not) you should see an underline below "Google" and e.g. ⌘-clicking the link will open it in your browser. Custom URI schemes can also be used, which makes it easy to cross-reference things in other apps. In iTerm2, this looks like the below screenshot, when the cursor is over "Google" and ⌘ is being held down. **What problem does it solved for you?** This would allow more seamless experience with hyperlinking e.g. Markdown content, or adding hyperlinks to items in the Tree view. This is useful for me specifically, since I want to use Rich for my OmniFocus python bindings to generate a task tree on the command-line, where each node in the tree is also a hyperlink with the `omnifocus://` URI scheme, to jump to that task from the CLI.

title: [REQUEST]Raw output method for Text Class
body:
**How would you improve Rich?**

As mentioned in #67 and #855, I think it would be useful to integrate the chocolate of rich with the peanut-butter of argparse.  I'm not super familiar with the code base but I think a way to get "most" of the way there would be to extend the Text class with a "raw" (or some more descriptive term) method that returns a string-type object with all escape-sequences and text exposed.  This would allow argparse to consume the contents of a rich.text.Text object and print the string and leave it up to the user's terminal to render.   I am sure there are other use-cases beyond argparse for this method too.

A simple example might look like:
```python
>>> foo = Text.assemble("foobar", style="red")
>>> foo.raw()
'\x1b[31mfoobar\x1b[00m'
```

**What problem does it solved for you?**

I think this could provide more options for integration.

title: [REQUEST] Extra caching for `get_character_cell_size`
body:
**How would you improve Rich?**

Add a small `lru_cache` to https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/blob/master/rich/cells.py#L28 , similar to cache one layer down for https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/blob/master/rich/cells.py#L46

Size `4096` was plenty for what I describe below.

**What problem does it solved for you?**

I'm working on some optimizations for a TUI application here https://github.com/JoshKarpel/spiel/pull/37

This was my first idea on how to improve rendering time, based on https://github.com/benfred/py-spy telling me that a lot of time was being spent in `get_character_cell_size`, and this was my first thought for a solution.

Adding the cache described above gives a ~30% speedup on the benchmarks I was using to work on that PR. In that application I'm repeatedly re-rendering the same content (in a `Live`), so adding a small cache to  `get_character_cell_size` represents a significant speedup since the set of characters is usually the same from frame to frame. The benchmark is mostly printing colorized ASCII, with some unicode also drawn from a small set (box-drawing characters, block shapes, etc.). 

I guess that since there's lots of `Layout` and `Padding` going on, the most common character is probably space... perhaps the ASCII set that there's already a shortcut for could just be pre-computed and stored in a set? There's probably a lot of good ways to approach this :)

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs) -> None:

title: [REQUEST] Auto-install features for rich.traceback (and possibly rich.pretty)
body:
[colored-traceback](https://github.com/staticshock/colored-traceback.py) does this thing where if you do `import colored_traceback.auto` it automatically calls `colored_traceback.install()` (actually `colored_traceback.add_hook()`). This is prettier than having `colored_traceback.install()`, and I think the same could be easily implemented with rich.traceback.

I was also thinking that the same could be done with something else like `rich.pretty`.

The way this is done is really simple. Just create a subfolder with an `__init__.py` file that calls `.install()`. See https://github.com/staticshock/colored-traceback.py/blob/master/colored_traceback/auto/__init__.py.

body:
While the progress() class is a nice and fairly easy to use, sometimes it is just the simpler 'track' function that's required. However, because it isn't possible to nicely print in a track function, it limits it's use cases.

It also means that if you try to write code that supports rich if available, but falls back to basic python without, you can't easily do it with progress class. With track you can simply add: `track = lambda x, *args, **kwargs : x` if rich is not available, but with a progress bar, you have to implement a full null context manager.

If possible, it would nice if you could pass track() the console object and it will print above the progress bar

title: [REQUEST] Support emoji variation selectors
body:
**How would you improve Rich?**

Add support for [variation selectors](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/38100329/some-emojis-e-g-have-two-unicode-u-u2601-and-u-u2601-ufe0f-what-does). I have recently stated using `rich` and want to migrate from the [emoji package](https://pypi.org/project/emoji/). However, the `emoji` package lets me specify a `variant_type` when printing. This will then append a sequence after every emoji to ensure that the correct variation is printed. See the `emoji` package [code in action](https://github.com/carpedm20/emoji/blob/70e7ba12dfaf3449a5d445b1e7de4ae2c6245d19/emoji/core.py#L72).

**What problem does it solve for you?**

Current behaviour:
```py
from rich.console import Console

def print_test():
    console = Console()
    console.print(":thumbs_up:")
    console.print(":warning:")
```
Results in:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9294862/123637993-8ceaa480-d816-11eb-92d8-696696c57e1f.png)

The equivellent code for the `emoji` package with `variant="emoji_type"` results in:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9294862/123638270-e521a680-d816-11eb-9a3d-9001955b77bb.png)

We can obtain this behaviour with `rich` by changing the code to
```py
console.print(":warning:\uFE0F")
```

But it would nice to have a flag on `Console` that automatically adds the sequence, so I don't have to append it every time an emoji doesn't render how I want it to.

title: [BUG] Progress(): Terminal size mis-detected if run in multiprocessing sub-process

**Describe the bug**
Using `multiprocessing` to run a sub process, initializing Progress() under that process fails to detect the terminal size, using the fallback (80, 25) instead.

**To Reproduce**
Sample code:
```
from multiprocessing import Process, Queue

from rich.console import Console
from rich.progress import Progress


def sub_process():
    pre_console = Console()
    print(f"Sub process PRE console size: {pre_console.size}\n")

    with Progress() as progress:
        print(f"Sub process progress.console.size: {progress.console.size}")

        console = Console()
        print(f"Sub process console size: {console.size}\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with Progress() as main_progress:

        print(f"Main progress.console.size: {main_progress.console.size}")

        main_console = Console()
        print(f"Main console size: {main_console.size}\n")

        q = Queue()
        process = Process(target=sub_process)
        process.start()
        process.join()

body:
**How would you improve Rich?**

I would like Rich to have its version included in the code — possibly in `__init__.__version__` — so that I can introspectively find the version of Rich installed.

rich

rich/10.5.0 (2021-05-07)
```

Cheers.

title: [REQUEST] Enable customization of repr() of built-in types, add hook points to enable customization of external classes (e.g. from other libraries) without `@auto` or monkey-patching `__rich_repr__`
body:
`rich` is amazing, and thank you @willmcgugan for creating it and the community around it.

# **Questionnaire**

* Consider posting in https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/discussions for feedback before raising a feature request.
  * This is almost certainly a terrible idea
  * I don't think community discussion would help here
  * I took a look and searched, but did not find anything relevant (searched for "quote" and "json")
* Have you checked the issues for a similar suggestions?
  *  I searched the issue tracker for any closed issues that mention "quote" or "json"
  *  I also spent a good amount of time with the docs and source code

# Preface

`rich.pretty.pprint` is amazing, I use it in so many things! My terminal is pretty, output is well-formatted, and coworkers look upon me with awe. 😉

One of those things is to print out objects consisting only of basic Python types (`str`, `int`, `list`, `dict`), which means that the output (after settings `indent_guides=False`) of `pprint` for an object heirarchy of these types is ALSO valid JSON! 🎉

...sometimes.

# Problem

JSON only accepts strings with double-quotes.  By default, Python's `str.__repr__` returns a string that uses single-quotes, unless the string *contains* a single quote but *does not* contain a double-quote.

This means that a very large percentage of strings will be single-quoted, which is **not valid JSON**.  This is annoying.

```python
>>> 'asdf'
'asdf'
>>> 'asdf"'
'asdf"'
>>> 'asdf\''
"asdf'"
>>> 'asdf\'\"'
'asdf\'"'
```

This can be more readily seen by actually using Python's `json` module.   Note the change in double-quotes to single-quotes.

```python
>>> json.loads('{"key": "value"}')
{'key': 'value'}
>>> json.loads("{'key': 'value'}")
JSONDecodeError: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)
```

title: [REQUEST] Support Basic Charts like bar or line.
body:
Consider posting in https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/discussions for feedback before raising a feature request.

- [x] Have you checked the issues for a similar suggestions?

**How would you improve Rich?**

If Rich support basic charts, it will be amazing!

There is a simple demo to draw a line chart on terminal.

```python3
# coding=utf-8
"""
曲线图

Line Graph
"""
import io
from .. import requirePackage

diagram = requirePackage('diagram')


class Line:
    def __init__(self, values: list, height: int, width: int):
        """
        折线图

        line chart

        :param values: 值列表
        :param height: 高度
        :param width: 宽度
        """
        self.values = values
        self.width = height
        self.height = width

    def __str__(self):
        """
        绘图并返回字符串

        Draw and return a string

        :return: 折线图的字符串
        """
        opt = diagram.DOption()
        opt.size = diagram.Point([self.height, self.width])
        opt.mode = 'g'
        stream = io.BytesIO()
        gram = diagram.DGWrapper(
            data=[self.values, range(len(self.values))],
            dg_option=opt,
            ostream=stream
        )
        gram.show()
        return str(stream.getvalue(), encoding="utf-8")

    def push(self, x: float):
        """
        尾部添加值

        Tail add value

        :param x: 值
        :return: None
        """
        self.values.append(x)

    def pop(self):
        """
        删除首部值

        Delete bow value

        :return: None
        """
        self.values.pop(0)

```

title: Tree: Flag to hide root from display
body:
In certain situations it would be useful to hide the root of a tree, either to save on screen space or for clarity. A `hide_root` flag could allow this behavior.  For example: 
```
>>> tree = Tree("Dir to print")
>>> tree.add("dir1").add("file1")
>>> tree.add("file2")
>>> print(tree)

Dir to print
├── dir1                                                                                     
│   └── file1                                                                                
└── file2                                                                                    
```
could instead be display as
```
>>> tree = Tree("Dir to print", hide_root=True)
>>> tree.add("dir1").add("file1")
>>> tree.add("file2")
>>> print(tree)

dir1                                                                                     
└── file1                                                                                
file2                                                                                    
```

Thanks!

title: [Docs] Outdated Render Group Documentation Examples
body:
The documentation for a [Render Group](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/group.html) includes the following two examples.

**One**

```python
from rich import print
from rich.console import Group
from rich.panel import Panel

panel_group = Group(
    Panel("Hello", style="on blue"),
    Panel("World", style="on red"),
)
print(Panel(panel_group))
```

**Two**

```python
from rich import print
from rich.console import group
from rich.panel import Panel

@group()
def get_panels():
    yield Panel("Hello", style="on blue")
    yield Panel("World", style="on red")

print(Panel(get_panels()))
```

Unless I am mistaken these examples will not work with the latest rich version since the class and decorator names have changed. In the current rich version the following examples would appear valid.

**One**

```python
from rich import print
from rich.console import RenderGroup
from rich.panel import Panel

panel_group = RenderGroup(
    Panel("Hello", style="on blue"),
    Panel("World", style="on red"),
)
print(Panel(panel_group))
```

**Two**

```python
from rich import print
from rich.console import render_group
from rich.panel import Panel

@render_group()
def get_panels():
    yield Panel("Hello", style="on blue")
    yield Panel("World", style="on red")

print(Panel(get_panels()))
```

title: [REQUEST] Suppress Tracebacks for libraries
body:
**How would you improve Rich?**

Rich has an excellent Traceback module that improves the formatting and readability of Tracebacks ✨ 

However, sometimes you don't just want nice formatting, you actually just want to **remove parts of the traceback**. This is most common when you are using infrastructure that you know is almost never "relevant" to the traceback itself.

It would be useful if it were possible to suppress Tracebacks for certain libraries/modules/etc, so that a traceback showed more relevant information for users (at the library author's discretion).

Some context in this twitter thread :-) https://twitter.com/willmcgugan/status/1439494982180737025

**What problem does it solve for you?**

There's a specific use-case here that might be quite common: using `rich` in combination with `click`. If you're using `click` to build your CLI, then tracebacks will dump several levels of `click` modules in addition to the error that is in your codebase. It would be most-useful to me if I could just say "Don't show any of the `click` stuff" :-)

**Did I help**

If I was able to resolve your problem, consider [sponsoring](https://github.com/sponsors/willmcgugan) my work on Rich, or [buy me a coffee](https://ko-fi.com/willmcgugan) to say thanks.

title: [BUG] Dataclass pretty repr can contain a trailing separator and whitespace
body:
When rich printing a dataclass:
If the last field has its `repr` disabled:  `repr=False`
Then, the pretty_repr will contain a trailing comma and whitespace.


**To Reproduce**
```py
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, fields
import rich
from rich import pretty, _loop

@dataclass
class ExpectedCase:
    first: bool = True
    _none: bool = field(init=False, repr=False)
    last: bool = True

@dataclass
class TrailingComma:
    first: bool = True
    last: bool = True
    _none: bool = field(init=False, repr=False)

if __name__ == '__main__':

    # demonstration
    rich.print(TrailingComma())

    # highlight
    trailing_repr = rich.pretty.pretty_repr(TrailingComma())
    print(' ' * (len(trailing_repr) - 4), '^^ \n')

    # show the issues source
    for example in [ExpectedCase(), TrailingComma()]:
        print('rich.print():  ', end='')
        rich.print(example)
        rich.print(f'rich f-string: {example}')
        print('builtin print:', example, '\n')

        print(f'dataclass Fields: ')
        example_fields = fields(example)
        for field in example_fields:
            rich.print(f'    {field.name!r:7} -> repr={field.repr}')
        print()

        print('rich._loop.loop_last() yields: ')
        for last, field in rich._loop.loop_last(example_fields):
            rich.print(f'    {last=!r:5}, field={field.name!r}')
        print()

        # possible to have no node marked as the last:
        print('rich.pretty.traverse() returns Nodes: ')
        for node in rich.pretty.traverse(example).children:
            rich.print(f'    {node.key_repr=}, {node.last=}')
        print('\n')
```

title: [REQUEST/IDEA] Tree Expand/Collapse
body:
### **How would you improve Rich?**

#### Background
So, I'm falling in love with `rich.tree.Tree` 😁 and have several nested trees (not unlike the results of the example: https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/blob/eb673d1204340738d3084ebc2e4c789a35a4e49b/examples/tree.py) 

#### The Improvement

Things are working great. The only thing that's a bit of a challenge is collapsing/expanding deeply nested trees. It would be awesome to have a couple of methods that would:

* Collapse all nested child tree elements (i.e. recursively set the `Tree.expanded = False` property of all children)
* Expand (reverse of above)
* Choose a depth (or depths, or all) on both of the above 

Effectively something like:
```python
#semi pseudocode
ftree = rich.tree.Tree() #result of the tree dir walk example?

ftree.collapse_all()
ftree.collapse(depth=1)

ftree.expand(depth=1)

#Maybe have an option to include parents of a certain depth too?
ftree.expand(depth=3, parents=True)
```
#### Implementation Notes/Ideas

Not sure which is better:
* Separate `collapse()` and `collapse_all()` methods?
* A single method with a parameter? e.g. `collapse(all=True)` (or maybe just `collapse()` implies all when called without a depth?)

### Other Thoughts
Relatedly, it would be kinda nice to have another mechanism to interact with children beyond a simple list. Maybe having the option to store children as a `dict` (with keys)? (Would be hepful to be able to recursively search children too... but maybe I'm getting a little far ahead 😉 ) 

### **What problem does it solve for you?**

Working with nested trees, convenience.

title: [BUG] Rich loghandler raising exceptions when using pythonw
body:
After switching to using the Rich log handler in an application it started raising `'NoneType' object has no attribute 'write'` exceptions, however, this would only happen when the debugger was not connected and running under _pythonw_ (the special windows version that does not create a console window, used for GUI applications).

`if raiseExceptions and sys.stderr:  # see issue 13807`

```python
import logging
from rich.logging import RichHandler

logging.basicConfig(handlers=[RichHandler()], level=logging.INFO)

try:
    logging.info("My amazing info message")
except Exception as ex:
    with open("error.txt", "w") as f_out:

title: [REQUEST] Add instructions about readline in the docs
body:
- [x] Have you checked the issues for similar suggestions.

I believe the docs (and the community in general) would benefit a **lot** from having some basic guidelines on how to use the standard [readline module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/readline.html) with Rich. It's a single import after all.

**What problem does it solve for you?**

Without `readline` (weird stuff are the result of arrow keys):
![withoutreadline](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/37125/139588643-81fa4b1e-8c99-43fc-aef1-ef52ee183477.gif)

With `readline`:
![withreadline](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/37125/139588648-7bd68d68-99af-43ff-b866-ef9ed52fce45.gif)

**How would you improve Rich?**

It turns out there's no need to change a single line in Rich, just mention it in the docs (such as [here](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/console.html?highlight=input#input)):

```python
from rich.console import Console
import readline  # just add this
console = Console()
console.input("What is [i]your[/i] [bold red]name[/]? :smiley: ")
```

The reason I think it is useful is because
1. it might not be known by beginners (I didn't!)
2. it's [nowhere to be found in the docs](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/search.html?q=readline&check_keywords=yes&area=default)
3. it's dead easy (just `import readline`)
4. similar stuff seems to have been requested before (e.g. #306), but without any definite answer

title: [REQUEST] pprint should sort unordered collections like `set()` and `dict()`
body:
**How would you improve Rich?**

`rich.pretty.pprint` should have the option to sort unordered collections like `set()` and `dict()`.

The same should be possible for the REPL via e.g. `pretty.install`.

**What problem does it solve for you?**

When in a REPL, after `rich.pretty.install()`, it would be nice if printing e.g. `dict` objects were sorted by key.

For compatibility reasons (and since Python3 dict objects are technically ordered by insertion order), this would probably be behind a new flag for `pprint` and `pretty.install`.

For example, it would be nice to have sorted keys for a `dict` ('ExampleToBreakLines' was added to force `pprint` to do line-breaks).

```
{
    'a': 1,
    'c': 3,
    'b': 2,
    'ExampleToBreakLines': 'AAAAAAAAAA...AAAAAAAAAAAA'
}
```

This may cause issues when the values-to-be-sorted (`dict` keys or `set` values) are not comparable (e.g. `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'`).  However, a best-effort would still be nice.

This should not violate the added functionality of types in `collections` e.g. `OrderedDict`:

```py
>>> isinstance(collections.OrderedDict, dict)
False
```

**Did I help**

Indeed you did help in the Discussions: https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/discussions/1651

title: [REQUEST] rich.inspect() should have a flag to show all contents of a module
body:
**How would you improve Rich?**

`rich.inspect()` is really, genuinely great.  I love it! ❤️ 

However, when used on modules, even with `method=True` (see #1658) , it leaves a lot to be desired.  It would be nice if there was a `module=True` flag or similar (even if it only works on `types.ModuleType`) that displays all properties of the module, and does this recursively (e.g. `toplevel.somemodule.SomeClass.some_class_method` would be displayed for `rich.inspect(toplevel.somemodule)`.  Things might get complicated if there are reference cycles (which are probably unlikely, but could be trivially constructed).*

Each object that might be displayed can have its `obj.__module__` checked against `somemodule.__name__` such that nice module documentation can be easily viewed.  The rules for `hidden` and `dunder` can continue to take the same effect that they do.

**What problem does it solve for you?**

I would like `inspect()` to be more useful when inspecting module types.

**What are the pitfalls?**

Cycles probably need to be prevented, so you'll probably need to keep track of the `id()` of all objects traversed to prevent cycles.  Something like this, for example:

```py
# mymodule.py

class MyClass:
    some_class_obj = None

MyClass. some_class_obj = MyClass
```

Or, even more trivially, which is handled correctly by Python's default `repr` and handled very slightly differently in `rich`'s `repr`.  So it does appear that `rich` does some level of `id()` tracking.

```
# Standard Python
>>> x = []
>>> x.append(x)
>>> x
[[...]]
```
```
# With rich.pretty.install()
>>> x = []
>>> x.append(x)
>>> x
[...]
```

title: [BUG!] Python script with Status adding new line to stdout with echo
body:
**Describe the bug**
In my company CI pipeline with GitHub Actions, recently a weird behavior started to appear when I ran a script that outputed a new environment variable with `print`:

```bash
echo "IMAGE_NAME=$(python -m buggy_deployment_manager --silent build $ENV .)" >> $GITHUB_ENV
```

This week or so, we've discovered it started to break all of our workflow jobs (GHA) with:

```
Error: Unable to process file command 'env' successfully.
Error: Invalid environment variable format '***.dkr.ecr.***.amazonaws.com/some-image-name'
```

Which usually happens when some unsupported character goes into the GITHUB_ENV file.

Going deep into the problem I found out that there was a newline being outputed to $GITHUB_ENV, although there was no print statement other than only one in the `buggy_deployment_manager` module, and no logging or etc was being held in the stdout buffer explicitly.

With pdb and flushing all print outputs, I've discovered that the context manager Status from rich actually (somehow and to somewhere) inside this `buggy_deployment_manager` prints out a newline to `echo` once it ends. This \n only appeared with `echo`, which is a weird behavior, I don't think it was supposed to happen or **why** it happened.

**To Reproduce**

Create a script named `bug.py` with:

```bug.py
from rich.status import Status
print("1 ", end="")
with Status("Go"):
    print("2 ", end="")
print("3 ", end="")
```

And run with:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
echo "WHAT=$(python bug.py)"
```

Instead of:
```
WHAT=1 2 3 
```

It will write:
```
WHAT=1 2 
3 
```

**Platform**

I've used locally on MacOS 12.0.1, Ubuntu 20.04 and within our CI runner ( Debian 11 ) with:
 - Python 3.8.10, 3.9.7, 3.9.8;

title: [BUG] tests: Equivalent objects fail __eq__ checks
body:
A mildly naive `__repr__` implementation on some objects leads to confusing results

Steps to reproduce
==================

Here is a copy+paste of a simple test case:
```
>>> from rich.style import Style
>>> from rich.text import Span
>>> Span(0,1,'bold')
Span(0, 1, 'bold')
>>> Span(0,1,Style(bold=True))
Span(0, 1, 'bold')
>>> Span(0,1,'bold') == Span(0,1,Style(bold=True))
False
```

Expected result
==============

The two `Span` objects should compare as equal.

Actual behaviour
================

The two `Span` objects compare as unequal, since the `str` and `Style` components are of differing types.

Errata
=====

* This is confusing in tests because the `__repr__` method on `Span` objects string-ifies the `Style` component, making them look completely equivalent; the net result is that tests will fail, and the provided diagnostic messages are of negative help.
* The `Span` object was used as an example, but there could be plenty more just like it in the codebase.

**Describe the bug**
The recent `typing-extensions` release is `4.0`. It is backward compatible, a team decided to use SemVer notation for the project.
rich is marked as compatible with `^3.7.4` which doesn't sail smoothly with other libraries.

Maybe the best solution is not pinning the top version and relay on `typing-extensions` stability.
Another option is pinning to `>=3.7.4, <5.0`.

I've tried to prepare a PR but found that `poetry lock` generates a very different lockfile than pushed on GitHub. 
So better to get help from @willmcgugan for this problem, the fix is really trivial.

title: [Bug/feature] Filename detection poor for paths/filenames with spaces
body:
rich's automatic highlighting for filenames is generally quite useful, but it tends to fail when the filename has a space in it. The highlighting breaks on the space.

```
my_filename = "/folder/file name.txt"
console.log(f"Scanning file {my_filename}")
```

This seems like a fairly tricky thing to get right, because obviously there's some ambiguity here that makes the grammar non-regular. For instance, you could image the string "/folder/file name.txt" could be either a folder named "/folder/file" and then an unrelated string "name.txt" or it could all be a filename.  I had a look at how rich.highlighter seems to operate and unsurprisingly it's just a battery of regexes.

I could think of two possible partial solutions here. The first would be to allow for a particular magic string that could surround a variable to indicate the entire variable should be parsed as a single syntax highlight, e.g. `console.log(f"Scanning file ||{my_filename}||")` or some such. The second would be -- is it possible to overload the default f-string processing (I don't know that I have a clear understanding of how f-strings are substituted at runtime to know if this is possible) to be able to make assumptions there.

Maybe these sorts of solutions add too much cruft to be worthwhile, but I figured I'd still raise the issue in case you have a cleverer sense than I do.

(Really love the package, I've converted a bunch of stuff to use it recently and am just totally impressed!)

title: [BUG] Live Progress Bars Double-Render in Jupyter Notebooks
body:
**Describe the bug**

Upgrading to `10.15.1` from `10.13.0` causes a double-render when using a live progress bar in a Jupyter Notebook. You can see this easily using the following example code:

```python
from rich.progress import Progress

with Progress() as progress:
    task1 = progress.add_task("[red]Downloading...", total=2)
    while not progress.finished:
        progress.update(task1, advance=1)
        progress.refresh()
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1581984/144648258-f5867cf2-be1b-40e3-a70a-919cc9bbd036.png)

If it matters, we were using `ipywidgets==7.6.5` for this example above. Rolling back to `rich==10.13.0` fixed the issue.

You can see the section below for a description of what's happening in the Jupyter messaging protocol, but my best guess is that the ipywidgets usage is slightly off and causing this bug.

**ipywidgets specifics**

Normally when you update an output widget it fires the following messages:
1. A `comm_msg` that specifies that all future messages apply to a specific output model
2. A `clear_output` message with `wait=True`
3. A `display_data` message including the new content
4. A `comm_msg` that specifies that future messages no longer apply to a specific output model

We were noticing that this is still the case except for the final update message, in which it does the following:

1. A `comm_msg` that specifies that all future messages apply to a specific output model
2. A `clear_output` message with `wait=True`
3. A `comm_msg` that specifies that future messages no longer apply to a specific output model
4. A `display_data` message including the new content

The swap of those two messages caused the double-render, because the old render is never cleared by an output to that widget model, and the display_data is tracked as a new output for the cell.


**Platform**

Underlying platform is linux, using the classic Jupyter interface. This also happened using Noteable's

body:
As a developer of network infrastructure testing systems I use Rich to display progress of testing using the logging feature and display reports using the Table feature.  In the same way that I use Text+Style to colorize my Tables, I would like to colorize/style text that is the logging output using the same Text/Style classes.  Presently the logging feature supports the "markup" color notation exclusively.  

This issue requests an enhancement so that I can pass Text objects to the logging log methods (info, error, warning, etc.) so that the output in the logs shows all color/styling that is supported by the Python logging infrastructure.  

Example desired usage; assume the variable "logger" is a Rich python logger instance:
````python
from rich.tex import Text, Style

name = Text("Jeremy", style=Style(color="blue"))
logger.info(f"Hello {name]")
````

The desired output would be "Hello Jeremy" with the text "Jeremy" colored blue.
